teaching assistant across our undergraduate and graduate sequences, and through
an annual R workshop series for graduate students.

## Statistics workshops for graduate students

Annual workshops for graduate students in Human Development and Family Sciences
at UT Austin, run through the departmental statistics committee.

::: {.course}
**AI-assisted data analysis: Vibe coding with Positron** [· January 2026]{.meta}

Working with an AI assistant inside a real analysis project: what it is good
at, where it fails silently, and the verification habits that make it safe on
research code.

::: {.entry-links}
[Slides](files/workshops/2026/vibe-coding-slides.pptx)
[Script](files/workshops/2026/pilot.R)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Data wrangling with R** [· January 2025]{.meta}

Reshaping, merging, and cleaning messy data.

::: {.entry-links}
[Script](files/workshops/2025/data-wrangling.Rmd)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Plotting figures with R** [· January 2024]{.meta}

Publication-quality figures in ggplot2, including legends, facets, fonts, and
export settings that survive a journal's production process.

::: {.entry-links}
[Slides](files/workshops/2024/figures-slides.pptx)
[Script](files/workshops/2024/figures-lecture.R)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Basic data analysis with R** [· January 2023]{.meta}

A first course for students who had only used SPSS: projects, scripts,
reproducibility, descriptives, and regression.

::: {.entry-links}
[R basics](files/workshops/2023/00-r-basics.R)
[Analysis with bruceR](files/workshops/2023/01-basic-analysis-bruceR.R)
:::
:::

In development: a workshop on the concepts underneath AI-assisted research,
covering tokens, context windows, agents, and the command line, for researchers
with no computing background.

Datasets are not posted. The examples use participant data that is not mine to
distribute, and I am rebuilding the exercises on synthetic data.

<figcaption>Engagement and the course overall are the two lowest items, while
the instructor-facing items are the highest.</figcaption>
:::

Three things I would do differently if I taught this course again.

**Know the program setting.** HDF 315L is a lower-division course, so I designed
it for lower-division students. Almost everyone who enrolled was a junior or
senior, with one exception. That mismatch drove the pacing and the amount of
scaffolding.

**Match the activity to the room.** I used group activities because they had
worked in the large child development lectures I assisted, where a group of four
is a way of making a hall of two hundred feel small. In a room of nine
upper-level students the same activity does the opposite: there is nothing to
break down, and asking students to turn to a group they are already sitting with
produced polite agreement rather than argument. What the graduate statistics
sections taught me is that small rooms run on individual commitment first, so I
am moving to written-first protocols where everyone answers before anyone
speaks, then pairs, then the whole room.

**Set expectations at the start, not along the way.** My clearest evaluations
have always been about feedback and responsiveness, which are things I do after
a student is already confused. What I did not do was tell students at the outset
what the course would ask of them, how the assignments connected, and what
counts as a good answer. A first-week overview of the arc of the course, and a
short written brief for each assignment, moves that work forward to where it
prevents confusion instead of repairing it.

In my first large lecture, the most common thing students wrote was that they
had not realised the course had a teaching assistant at all. Being noticeable in
a room of two hundred is a skill, and I did not have it. I learned to arrive
before class, introduce myself out loud in the first week, say when my office
hours were rather than only posting them, and stay behind afterwards. By Fall
2024 almost nobody said they had not noticed me, and being easy to reach had
become the thing students mentioned most.

Grading changed the same way. Early on, students said my marking was too harsh
and did not match the instructor's. The fix was not to mark more gently. It was
to agree the standard with the instructor before the first assignment, mark
against a written rubric, and say in the comment what each deduction was for.
Students still sometimes call me strict, which I am fine with now that it is
predictable and explained.

One problem is not solved. In every class, a few students say they got almost
nothing from me while others in the same room say I was the most useful support
they had. Those students never came to office hours and never emailed. Being
available did not reach them, because the students who most need help are the
least likely to ask for it. Waiting to be asked is itself a decision, and I need
to go to them instead: a short check-in message to anyone who has not been in
touch, and one required brief meeting early in the semester.

## Mentoring

In the [BSEC Lab](https://hdfs.utexas.edu/directory/nicole-perry) I supervised
an undergraduate through to a presentation at the university's undergraduate
research forum. I also supervise undergraduates in the
[MOSAIC Lab](https://sites.utexas.edu/mosaiclab/).

I train graduate and undergraduate assistants in physiological data collection
and preprocessing: RSA acquisition with Mindware, behavioural coding with
Mangold Interact, and the cleaning pipelines that follow.
